transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-22
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Kyros ML Lead), Ravi Menon (Kyros Infra), Tomasz Kowalski (Kyros CTO)

Summary: Quick technical deep dive on quantization options (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ), expected quality regressions, and deployment constraints for an on-prem / VPC private deployment. Customer wants latency < 120ms 95p for 2k token generations and >800 tokens/s throughput for batch workloads. Focus on KV cache behavior and batching tradeoffs when using quantized kernels.

Topics: INT8 vs FP8 accuracy tradeoffs, GPTQ/GPTQ-like conversion artifacts, AWQ operational maturity, batching strategies, KV cache hotpath, memory/throughput on Kyros hardware (A100-ish and some older T4), VPC/on-prem integration and KMS, benchmark plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll give a quick agenda — samir is going to walk through the quantization tradeoffs and then we'll go into perf numbers, ok?
[00:12] Elena: thanks, yeah we've been doing internal experiments, mostly 8-bit and some GPTQ conversions; curious about tradeoffs like inference speed vs accuracy and how cache interacts.
[00:23] Samir: cool, great. quick note: some of my terms might come out a bit shorthand — awq, g p t q, those are the conversions we've been using. so first, INT8 — it's the lowest-effort path in many runtimes, but you often trade off accuracy unless you do per-channel scale or symmetric quant. that matters more on instruction-following workloads.
[00:45] Ravi: when you say "lowest effort" what exactly do you mean? less postop?
[00:50] Samir: right — typically INT8 workflows require fewer weight transforms and the kernels are more mature; many runtimes have fast INT8 GEMM kernels and they support continuous batching nicely. conversions like GPTQ and AWQ sit on top of int8-ish representations but they do more per-layer reconstruction.
[01:08] Tomasz: what about FP8? we've heard FP8 can give better fidelity than int8 with comparable memory savings on newer hardware that supports it.
[01:16] Samir: FP8 is promising, yes — especially FP8 formats (E4M3/E5M2 depending on vendor). the caveat is hardware support: on A100 you don't have native FP8 — newer H100/Hopper do. so if your on-prem fleet has mixed generation, FP8 may not be practical. also software kernels for fp8 are still evolving, so perf might be variable.
[01:38] Elena: our fleet is mostly A100 and some T4s, so FP8 is probably out.
[01:44] Morgan: that aligns — most customers with mixed infra prefer INT8+GPTQ/AWQ path.
[01:49] [01:49] Samir: quick thing about GPTQ — it's a post-training quantization that tries to minimize MSE by reconstructing activations per channel; generally lower reg compared to naive int8, but it's sensitive: dataset used to calibrate matters a lot. we've seen cases where GPTQ reduces perplexity but for instruction-tuned models you can still get odd hallucination regressions if calibration set didn't include relevant prompts.
[02:12] Elena: ah yeah we saw that, small but noticeable drop on our instruction evals. is that typical?
[02:17] Samir: yes it's common. AWQ is another approach — it often achieves better accuracy for 8-bit like workloads on LLMs because it includes block-wise quant and some per-block compensation. the tradeoff is encoding complexity and sometimes larger kernels.
[02:33] Ravi: perf-wise, do GPTQ/AWQ hurt latency or help it? we care about p95 latency for single-request flows.
[02:42] Samir: in general, inference latency is comparable or slightly better with GPTQ compared to naive int8 as GPTQ enables denser math and smaller memory footprint which helps cache locality. AWQ can be a little heavier on compute if the kernels aren't fused, but on good kernels it can match or beat GPTQ for some models. key is kernel maturity on your runtime.
[03:02] Morgan: and Redwood's runtime — we have optimized kernels for INT8 and GPTQ variants, we've also got AWQ experiments. for on-prem we can bring the same kernel stack but need to validate on your exact CUDA/cuDNN drivers.
[03:16] [03:16] Tomasz: what about KV cache? we've noticed memory spikes when using quantized models with long-context use; does quantization change KV cache behavior?
[03:26] Samir: good question. quantization mostly affects weight and activation storage. KV cache remains FP16 or FP32 in most runtimes — because it's accumulated key/value states. you can quantize KV cache but that introduces latency and accuracy tradeoffs. so in Redwood's runtime we keep KV cache in fp16 by default to preserve attention quality and to keep update logic simple. that means your per-token memory for cache isn't reduced as much as weights, but overall model memory drops substantially.
[03:52] Elena: okay so memory for weights down, but KV still significant. our p95 latency budget is tight, so we worry about the extra memory bandwidth.
[04:02] Samir: this is where batching and continuous batching helps — if you have micro-batching or serverless-like singletons, the KV cache hotpath dominates. we optimize pre-allocations and make KV updates incremental; for batch workloads you get much better throughput because attention can reuse cached keys.
[04:24] Ravi: can you explain how batching size impacts latency in your runtime with quantized kernels?
[04:30] Samir: sure — smaller batch sizes favor single-request latency but hurt throughput. quantized kernels often have smaller memory footprints so they can fit larger effective batch sizes before hitting memory limits, which improves throughput. but the per-request p95 might still increase if kernel dispatch overhead grows. our profiling shows a knee around batch 4-8 for 2k token runs on A100 in INT8; that knee shifts a bit with GPTQ/AWQ.
[04:56] Elena: knee meaning the point where throughput starts to scale well?
[04:59] Samir: exactly. before that point you don't amortize kernel launch cost enough.
[05:05] [05:05] Morgan: can i interject — for Kyros' SLA (120ms p95 for 2k tokens) that's very aggressive, we might need dedicated reserved capacity with pinning to achieve it.
[05:15] Tomasz: yeah we were thinking dedicated GPUs, probably reserved, some on-prem. pricing will weigh in.
[05:20] Morgan: we'll send reserved pricing but also propose an architecture: host a lightweight serving tier in your VPC with Redwood Private control plane in a peered VPC; that lets us keep keys in your KMS and keeps logs local.
[05:36] Ravi: KMS — do you support external HSM or bring-your-own keys?
[05:40] Morgan: yes we support BYOK via KMIP/HSM integrations and common cloud KMS providers; we'll share the security doc.
[05:47] [05:47] Samir: back to perf — another dimension is quantization-induced kernel memory access patterns. some int8 kernels are memory-bound on older GPUs (T4), so throughput gains are smaller there. on A100, compute-bound kernels can exploit tensor cores and provide much better throughput improvement.
[06:06] Elena: do you have numbers roughly? like tokens/sec uplift with GPTQ vs fp16?
[06:11] Samir: ballpark for a Llama2-13B-like model: FP16 baseline ~350-450 tokens/s on an A100 depending on seq length; INT8/GPTQ optimized kernel can hit 700-900 tokens/s in our tests with batch sizes tuned. AWQ sometimes pushes to 800-1,000 depending on kernel fusion. these are rough, real numbers depend on prompt length and attention pattern.
[06:37] Tomasz: that's useful. but our concern is accuracy — can you share expected eval delta on instruction-following tasks?
[06:45] Samir: typical GPTQ delta on instruction evals is 1-3% relative score drop if calibration is good; worst-case outliers can be 5-7% if calibration set is mismatched. AWQ often reduces that gap to <1-2% for many models but it's model-dependent. again, we provide per-prompt eval harness to compute regressions on your testset.
[07:06] [07:06] Ravi: what about mixed-precision strategies? are you recommending hybrid fp16 weights + int8 activations?
[07:12] Samir: yes hybrid schemes are common: keep sensitive layers in FP16 (output or first/last attention blocks) and quantize the rest. This reduces regression while preserving most perf gains. Redwood's optimize tool can suggest which layers to keep in full precision based on sensitivity analysis.
[07:31] Elena: can Redwood run the sensitivity analysis on our model offline?
[07:34] Morgan: yes, we can run that as part of the pilot. we'll need a model binary or a reproducible conversion step. for security we can run it in your VPC.
[07:44] [07:44] Samir: also worth calling out runtime fallback policies — if a QA regression is detected during rollout we can auto-fallback to a higher-precision variant or previous model; that keeps prod safe.
[07:56] Tomasz: good. about on-prem deployment — how invasive is the install, and can we keep logs/audit inside our network?
[08:03] Morgan: Redwood Private can be deployed with a customer-managed control plane; logs and telemetry can be optionally stored in your S3 or local object store, and audit events are shipped to your SIEM. we'll share the installation matrix; typical installs take 2-5 days for a small cluster with our infra team.
[08:20] Ravi: kernel compatibility has bitten us before — driver versions etc. what's required?
[08:24] Samir: we require CUDA 11.8+ for our optimized kernels and specific cuDNN versions; we'll provide a driver/stack matrix. part of onboarding is a preflight script that collects versions and we validate.
[08:35] [08:35] Elena: for the calibration data for GPTQ — is it okay to use synthetic prompts or we should use our real user prompts?
[08:42] Samir: real user prompts or a representative subset are best; synthetic sets often miss interactive patterns. even a few thousand diverse prompts that reflect instruction variants helps.
[08:53] Morgan: if needed we can help filter and sample your logs in a privacy-preserving way.
[08:59] [08:59] Tomasz: any pitfalls we should be aware of when doing on-prem conversion and rolling to prod?
[09:04] Samir: yes — common pitfalls: 1) calibration set mismatch causing edge-case regressions, 2) mixed hardware fleet — some devices won't run the same kernels or will have performance cliffs, 3) KV cache memory underestimated because weight savings are not equal to runtime memory saving, 4) shipping logs for eval incorrectly labeled. we put guardrails in the rollout pipeline to detect these.
[09:29] Elena: for edge-case regressions, can we do A/B testing per route?
[09:33] Morgan: yes — Redwood supports per-route rollouts and canary percentages, with automatic rollback on quality triggers.
[09:39] [09:39] Ravi: about storage — how big are model artifacts after GPTQ/AWQ conversion compared to FP16?
[09:45] Samir: converted artifacts are typically 2-4x smaller than FP16 depending on block sizes; INT8 can be roughly half to a quarter the bytes of FP16. GPTQ tends to compress more effectively because of reconstruction tables, AWQ can trade slightly larger artifacts for better quality.
[10:00] Tomasz: okay. we have some regulatory constraints: logs must be kept for 3 years, and access controlled. is that supported?
[10:07] Morgan: yes, audit retention and RBAC are configurable; for Private deployments you can fully control retention via your object store.
[10:13] [10:13] Samir: another note — tokenization edgecases can amplify quantization regressions if your calibration set doesn't include rare tokens. include representative token distribution.
[10:22] Elena: good point. we'll gather a 10k prompt sample from last quarter.
[10:27] Morgan: perfect. next, benchmarks — proposed plan: Samir runs INT8/GPTQ/AWQ baseline on our side with a model similar to yours, then run the conversion in your VPC on a small cluster to reproduce numbers. we should also test long context 4k+ since you mentioned long sessions.
[10:44] Samir: yes, we'll do both short and long context tests. for long context KV cache footprint becomes dominant; we'll provide memory vs latency curves.
[10:53] [10:53] Ravi: for the on-prem run, what data do you need from us?
[10:57] Morgan: model binary (or a path), cuda/driver versions, sample requests, and a small dataset for calibration. we'll provide an SFTP/transfer playbook.
[11:07] Tomasz: we'd prefer the work to happen inside our VPC — can Redwood execute conversions there?
[11:11] Morgan: yes, we can run conversions in your VPC with an outbound-restricted agent; results and artifacts remain in your storage.
[11:18] [11:18] Elena: is there a cost estimate for the conversion work and pilot?
[11:21] Morgan: we'll send a pilot quote — typically it's a time-and-materials engagement plus compute usage; for larger pilots we offer a small credit against reserved capacity.
[11:29] Samir: technical detail: when doing GPTQ we sometimes observe a small accuracy cliff in some generation heuristics — e.g., temperature sensitivity changes slightly; it's important to re-tune sampling params post-conversion.
[11:44] Elena: we can do that. we'll want to keep production determinism.
[11:47] Samir: ok then re-tune is part of the rollout checklist.
[11:51] [11:51] Morgan: any other blockers on your side?
[11:54] Ravi: just driver matrix and access to a dev cluster — i'll share a VM and creds.
[11:58] Tomasz: timeline wise, we'd like a pilot in early january.
[12:02] Morgan: great, we'll target Jan 6 for the on-prem benchmark.
[12:06] [12:06] Elena: one more question — what's Redwood's approach to monitoring quality drift post-quantization?
[12:11] Samir: we integrate eval hooks in the runtime; you can define prompt sets and quality thresholds. we run periodic evals and trigger alerts or rollbacks on regressions. also provide per-token confidence heuristics and delta tracking.
[12:25] Morgan: we'll include the eval dashboard in the pilot deliverables.
[12:29] [12:29] Tomasz: ok that's helpful.
[12:31] Morgan: wrapping up — action items and next steps as we discussed. we'll follow up with the AWQ/GPTQ spreadsheet and the security doc. thanks everyone.
[12:41] Elena: thanks, bye.
[12:42] Ravi: thanks.

End of transcript.
